name: Product & Digital Analytics
tagline: Active users, new users, DAU and stickiness, sessions, engagement, conversion, retention and installs for apps and websites
description: Event exports from product-analytics tools (Mixpanel, Amplitude, PostHog, Heap, Pendo, Segment), the GA4 and Firebase BigQuery export, Indian engagement platforms (CleverTap, MoEngage, WebEngage, Netcore), session tables, user tables with first-seen, last-seen and retention flags, and daily app statistics from Google Play Console, App Store Connect, Firebase and AppsFlyer.

fields.label: User ID
fields.description: Identifies each user; repeats on every event, session or day the user was active.

fields.label: Event time
fields.description: When each event happened, with its time of day.

fields.label: Date
fields.description: Calendar day of the activity: the day of an event, or the day a row of daily statistics covers.

fields.label: Active installs (installed base)
fields.description: Devices or users with the app installed on a day: a running total, read on the latest day and never summed.

subDomains.name: Event log
subDomains.description: One row per tracked event (or per event per day) with the user, the event name, when it happened and properties such as platform, device, page and country, as exported from Mixpanel, Amplitude, PostHog, Segment or the GA4 BigQuery export.

subDomains.name: Sessions
subDomains.description: One row per visit or app session with the user, start time, duration, pages or screens viewed, traffic source and whether it bounced, engaged or converted.

subDomains.name: User table
subDomains.description: One row per user with sign-up or first-seen date, last-seen date, platform, lifetime sessions or events, paying status and retention flags (including A/B-test user tables).

subDomains.name: Daily app statistics
subDomains.description: One row per day (per app, platform or country) with installs, uninstalls, active users, new users, sessions and crashes, as in Google Play Console, App Store Connect, Firebase and AppsFlyer reports.

kpis.name: Active users
kpis.definition: Distinct users who did anything tracked in the period: an event, a screen view or a session.

variants.label: Distinct device IDs
variants.caveat: No user ID column, so devices are counted: one person on two devices counts twice.

pitfalls: Recounted for every period and group, so the users of two days or two platforms never add up to the total.

kpis.name: Users
kpis.definition: Users in the table; with a date range, the users who signed up or were first seen in it.

variants.label: Row count (no user ID)
variants.caveat: No user ID column, so every row is counted as one user. Check the grain.

kpis.name: Events
kpis.definition: Tracked events in the period: page and screen views, clicks, purchases and every other action the product logs.
kpis.formula: Sum of the event count column, or one per row of an event log

variants.label: Rows (one per event)
variants.caveat: No event count column, so each row is counted as one event.

pitfalls: Event volume moves with tracking changes (a new event, autocapture switched on) as much as with real usage.

kpis.name: New users
kpis.definition: Users who used the product for the first time in the period: a first open, first visit or sign-up.
kpis.formula: New-users column, else distinct users with a first-open or sign-up event, else users first seen in the period

variants.label: Users with a first-open or sign-up event
Users first seen in the period
variants.caveat: Counts users whose first event in this file falls in the period, so the file's first weeks count everyone as new.

kpis.name: Average DAU
kpis.definition: Average number of distinct users active per day over the period.
kpis.formula: Distinct users per day (or the DAU column's daily total), averaged over the days in the period

variants.label: DAU column totalled per day, averaged

pitfalls: Days with no activity at all are missing from the file, so they are not averaged in.
Needs a date column without times; a timestamp alone cannot be read as days.

kpis.name: User conversion rate
kpis.definition: Share of active users who completed a key conversion event, such as a purchase, a subscription or a trial start.
kpis.formula: Users with a conversion event ÷ active users

variants.label: Users with a conversion event ÷ active users
Users with revenue ÷ active users
variants.caveat: No conversion events recognised, so users with any revenue count as converted.

pitfalls: Which events count as conversions is set in Check & map › Value meanings; check them before comparing with another tool's figure.

kpis.name: Sessions
kpis.definition: Visits or app sessions in the period.
kpis.formula: Distinct session IDs, or the sum of a sessions column

variants.label: Rows with a session start
variants.caveat: No session ID, so each row with a session start time is counted as one session.

pitfalls: In GA4 exports a session ID is only unique within its user, so distinct session IDs can run slightly low.

kpis.name: Avg session duration (minutes)
kpis.definition: Average time spent per session, in minutes.
pitfalls: Tools time the last page of a session differently (Universal Analytics counted a bounce as zero seconds), so durations compare only within one tool.

kpis.name: Bounce rate
kpis.definition: Share of sessions that left after a single page or without engaging.

variants.label: Sessions not engaged ÷ sessions
variants.caveat: GA4's definition: sessions that were not engaged.

variants.label: Single-page sessions ÷ sessions
variants.caveat: No bounce flag, so sessions with exactly one page or screen view count as bounces.

pitfalls: Universal Analytics and GA4 define a bounce differently, so rates from before and after the switch do not compare.

kpis.name: Pages per session
kpis.definition: Average number of pages or screens viewed per session.

kpis.name: Installs
kpis.definition: New installs of the app in the period, as reported by the store console or attribution tool.
pitfalls: Store consoles count device installs and user installs separately; keep to one of them.

kpis.name: Uninstall rate
kpis.definition: Uninstalls in the period as a share of installs in the same period.
pitfalls: A period's uninstalls come partly from earlier installs, so this compares two flows; it is not the share of new installs later removed.

kpis.name: Day-1 retention
kpis.definition: Share of users who came back the day after they first used the product.

variants.label: Users last seen 1+ days after first seen
variants.caveat: No retention flag, so users last seen at least a day after they were first seen count as retained (day 1 or later).

pitfalls: Users who joined in the last day of the data have not had the chance to return yet.

kpis.name: Day-7 retention
kpis.definition: Share of users who came back seven days after they first used the product.

variants.label: Users last seen 7+ days after first seen
variants.caveat: No retention flag, so users last seen at least seven days after they were first seen count as retained (day 7 or later).

pitfalls: Users who joined in the last week of the data have not had the chance to return yet, so recent cohorts look worse.

kpis.name: Day-30 retention
kpis.definition: Share of users who came back 30 days after they first used the product.

variants.label: Users last seen 30+ days after first seen
variants.caveat: No retention flag, so users last seen at least 30 days after they were first seen count as retained (day 30 or later).

pitfalls: Users who joined in the last month of the data have not had the chance to return yet, so recent cohorts look worse.

kpis.name: Paying users %
kpis.definition: Share of users who pay: a purchase, a subscription or a paid plan.

variants.label: Users with revenue ÷ users
variants.caveat: No paying flag, so users with any revenue count as paying.

kpis.name: Average active span
aliases: Days from first to last seen
kpis.definition: Average days between a user's first and last activity.
kpis.formula: Average of last seen − first seen, in days
pitfalls: Recent sign-ups have had little time to build a span, so newer cohorts always look shorter.

kpis.name: Events per user
kpis.definition: Average number of tracked events per active user.

kpis.name: Events per session
kpis.definition: Average number of tracked events per session.

kpis.name: Returning users %
kpis.definition: Share of active users who were active on two or more different days in the period.
kpis.formula: Users active on 2+ days ÷ active users

variants.label: Users active on two or more days (event time)
Users active on two or more days (date)
Users with sessions on two or more days

pitfalls: A longer period leaves more days to come back in, so compare periods of equal length.

kpis.name: Stickiness (DAU/MAU)
kpis.definition: How many of the month's users come back on a typical day: average daily users as a share of monthly users.

variants.label: Average DAU ÷ active users
variants.caveat: Read it per month: over a longer range the denominator holds everyone active in the whole range.

benchmark.note: Indicative: many consumer apps sit around 10–20%; messaging and social apps run far higher, tools used weekly lower.

kpis.name: Engagement time per user (minutes)
aliases: Average engagement time per active user
kpis.definition: Average minutes of engaged time per active user in the period.

kpis.name: Sessions per user
kpis.definition: Average number of sessions per user.

variants.label: Sessions ÷ users (rows)
variants.caveat: No user ID column, so each row is taken as one user.

kpis.name: Page and screen views
kpis.definition: Pages and app screens viewed in the period.
kpis.formula: Sum of page or screen views, or count of page-view events

kpis.name: Engagement rate
kpis.definition: Share of sessions that engaged: lasted a while, viewed more than one page or converted.

variants.label: Sessions that did not bounce
variants.caveat: No engagement flag, so sessions that did not bounce count as engaged.

kpis.name: Session conversion rate
kpis.definition: Share of sessions that included a conversion.

variants.label: Sessions with revenue ÷ sessions
variants.caveat: No conversion flag, so sessions with any revenue count as converted.

kpis.name: Revenue
kpis.definition: Revenue recorded by the product: purchases, subscriptions and in-app or ad revenue.
pitfalls: Analytics revenue is what the app reported, before refunds and store fees; finance figures will differ.

kpis.name: Revenue per user
kpis.definition: Revenue divided across all users, paying or not.

variants.label: Revenue ÷ users (rows)
variants.caveat: No user ID column, so each row is taken as one user.

kpis.name: Paying users
kpis.definition: Users who pay: a purchase, a subscription or a paid plan.

variants.label: Users with revenue
variants.caveat: No paying flag, so users with any revenue count as paying.

kpis.name: Revenue per paying user
kpis.definition: Revenue divided across the users who pay.

kpis.name: Net installs
kpis.definition: Installs minus uninstalls in the period: how much the installed base grew.

kpis.name: Uninstalls
kpis.definition: App uninstalls in the period.

kpis.name: Crashes per 1,000 sessions
kpis.definition: App crashes for every thousand sessions.

kpis.name: Game rounds per user
kpis.definition: Average game rounds or levels played per user.

kpis.name: Active installs
kpis.definition: Devices or users with the app installed on the latest day of the period.
kpis.formula: Installed base on the latest date

variants.label: Installed base on the latest date

pitfalls: A running total: it is read on the last day of each period, never added up across days.

kpis.name: Distinct events
kpis.definition: Number of different event names logged in the period.

kpis.name: Devices
kpis.definition: Distinct devices active in the period.

charts.title: Active users over time
charts.reason: Distinct users per period, recounted for each period and never summed across days, read best as a line.

charts.title: Events over time
charts.reason: Event counts per period are totals, so columns from a zero baseline compare them honestly.

charts.title: New users over time
charts.reason: New users per period are discrete counts: columns show acquisition rising or falling.

charts.title: Average daily active users
charts.reason: DAU averaged over the days of each period: a line shows whether daily use is growing without summing users across days.

charts.title: Stickiness (DAU/MAU)
charts.reason: A ratio recomputed for each month: a line shows whether users are coming back more often.

charts.title: Events by name
charts.reason: One count across many named events: sorted horizontal bars keep the names readable. Top 15 plus Others.

charts.title: Active users by platform
charts.reason: Distinct users per platform; a person on two platforms counts in each, so bars rather than a part-to-whole donut.

charts.title: Active users by country
charts.reason: Users across many countries: sorted bars of the top 10, with Others recounted rather than summed.

charts.title: Users by feature
charts.reason: Feature adoption: how many distinct users touched each feature, sorted so the most and least used stand out.

charts.title: Top pages and screens
charts.reason: Distinct users per page or screen, sorted: shows where people spend their visits.

charts.title: When users are active
charts.reason: Two time dimensions and one count: a weekday × hour heatmap shows when people use the product, for releases and notifications.

charts.title: User conversion rate by platform
charts.reason: A rate compared across a few platforms: bars of the recomputed conversion rate, with platforms under 30 rows hidden as too small.

charts.title: User conversion rate by source
charts.reason: Which acquisition sources bring users who convert: sorted bars of the recomputed rate, small sources hidden.

charts.title: Event catalogue
charts.reason: Several measures per event: a sortable table shows volume and reach side by side.

charts.title: Results by experiment variant
charts.reason: An A/B test compares a few variants on several measures: a table keeps them side by side.

charts.title: Sessions over time
charts.reason: Sessions per period are totals, so columns from a zero baseline compare them honestly.

charts.title: Session duration
charts.reason: An average duration recomputed for each period from its sessions, as a line.

charts.title: Bounce rate over time
charts.reason: A rate recomputed for each period from its sessions, drawn as a line and never averaged across days.

charts.title: Sessions by source
charts.reason: Where visits come from: sorted bars of the top 10 sources plus Others.

charts.title: Sessions by device
charts.reason: Each session has one device, so a donut shows the split between mobile, desktop and tablet at a glance.

charts.title: Bounce rate by landing page
charts.reason: A rate compared across pages: sorted bars of the recomputed bounce rate, with pages under 30 sessions hidden.

charts.title: Session conversion rate by source
charts.reason: Which sources bring visits that convert: sorted bars of the recomputed rate, small sources hidden.

charts.title: Distribution of session duration
charts.reason: Session lengths are skewed: a histogram shows the many short visits and the long tail that an average hides.

charts.title: When sessions start
charts.reason: A weekday × hour heatmap of sessions shows the busiest times.

charts.title: Source performance
charts.reason: Several measures per source: a sortable table carries more than any single chart.

charts.title: New users by sign-up month
charts.reason: Users counted by when they signed up or were first seen: columns show the size of each cohort.

charts.title: Day-7 retention by sign-up month
charts.reason: Retention recomputed for each sign-up month: a line shows whether newer cohorts stick better than older ones.

charts.title: Users by platform
charts.reason: One row per user and one platform each: a donut shows the split at a glance.

charts.title: Users by country
charts.reason: Users across many countries: sorted bars of the top 10 plus Others.

charts.title: Retention by experiment variant
charts.reason: An A/B test on retention: day-1 and day-7 rates side by side for each variant, on one percentage axis.

charts.title: Day-7 retention by source
charts.reason: Which sources bring users who stay: sorted bars of the recomputed rate, sources under 30 users hidden.

charts.title: Paying users % by platform
charts.reason: A rate across a few platforms: bars of the recomputed share, small platforms hidden.

charts.title: Days from first to last seen
charts.reason: How long users stay: a histogram shows the many who leave on day one and the loyal tail.

charts.title: Results by experiment variant
charts.reason: An A/B test compares a few variants on several measures: a table keeps them side by side.

charts.title: Installs and uninstalls
charts.reason: Two counts in the same unit over time: one line each shows whether installs outpace removals.

charts.title: New users over time
charts.reason: New users per period are totals: columns from a zero baseline compare them honestly.

charts.title: Installs by country
charts.reason: Installs across many countries: sorted bars of the top 10 plus Others.

charts.title: Installs by app or platform
charts.reason: Part-to-whole across a handful of apps: a donut shows the split at a glance.

charts.title: Installs by platform
charts.reason: Part-to-whole across Android, iOS and other platforms: a donut shows the split at a glance.

charts.title: Crashes per 1,000 sessions by app version
charts.reason: A rate across releases: sorted bars of the recomputed crash rate show which versions are unstable.

charts.title: Uninstall rate by country
charts.reason: A rate compared across countries: sorted bars of uninstalls ÷ installs, recomputed for each.

charts.title: Country performance
charts.reason: Several measures per country: a sortable table carries more than any single chart.

pitfalls: Distinct users never add up across days, platforms or countries: they are recounted for every period and group, so DAU, WAU and MAU are never summed.
A file's first weeks make everyone look new and retention look low: first-seen dates only start where the export starts.
Identity is often split: one person can appear as an anonymous device ID and a logged-in user ID, which inflates user counts.
Event volume moves with tracking changes as much as with usage; compare users and rates rather than raw event counts across a tracking change.
Bots, internal staff and test devices inflate counts; filter them out before reading trends.
Rates such as conversion, bounce and retention are recomputed from counts for every period and group, never averaged across days or platforms.
